doc.title: Sheryl Bailey interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 24, 2023

title: Hearing Sonny Rollins, Parker and Wes on WYEP; Pittsburgh guitar scene
summary: Bailey was hooked on jazz by public radio in Pittsburgh, got a teacher through her mother, and saw visiting guitarists via Joe Negri.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Well said. Was there a particular artist and even beyond that a particular LP that put you on the jazz path?

Yeah, well you know I’m from the Pittsburgh area and there was a radio station back when you had way more independent radio stations, WYEP, and they had all kinds of — it was public access radio. And you know I just listened to all kinds of things there. And I turned it on and I heard Sonny Rollins. And then I heard Charlie Parker. And then I heard Wes Montgomery. And then I just was hooked. It was an addiction from there. So then I started — my mother actually — at the time I was playing in a rock band and my grades were terrible. I mean I was playing gigs in bars. I was a teenager. And I said well that’s what I’m going to do. And my mother said, “Well you have to study.” You know, “You’re going to go to school for this.” I said, “Okay, okay.” So she introduced me to a teacher, his name is John Mayone in Pittsburgh, and so through him he made me recordings of Jimmy Raney, Wes Montgomery, and Herb Ellis. And at that time they were cassette tapes and they were sort of collections of things. And Joe Pass. And actually in Pittsburgh at that time there were a lot of — Joe Pass — I used to see him a lot. I would see Tal Farlow, I saw Herb Ellis. They would come through because of Joe Negri from Mr. Rogers Neighborhood. That was a Pittsburgh community. And through handyman Joe Negri all these great jazz artists and jazz guitarists would come through Pittsburgh. So anyway just that experience, and then it became something that, you know me and my mom would do — go, “Hey, who’s playing in town.” We saw Ella and we saw Andre Previn, we saw Mel Torme, you know whoever that was — so that was my experience getting into jazz. But the early recordings were those folks you know. Jimmy Raney for sure and Charlie Parker.
